accroche: Weber does not say the world has become less mysterious: he says we can now do without it, which is not the same thing.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 7, 1917, in Munich, in a lecture series organized for students disoriented by three years of war, the sociologist Max Weber gave a famous address, *Wissenschaft als Beruf*, “the profession and vocation of the scholar.” In it he uttered a phrase that would run through the entire following century: the fate of our era, marked by rationalization and intellectualization, is characterized above all by what he calls the “disenchantment of the world.”

## The mechanism

The German expression, *Entzauberung*, literally means “demagification.” It does not mean that the inhabitants of the modern world understand more about what surrounds them than their ancestors did. A city dweller who takes the streetcar generally knows no more about the laws of electricity than a hunter-gatherer understood the forces he believed he had to appease. The difference, Weber insists, lies elsewhere: one can now, in principle, master everything by calculation. One no longer needs to resort to magical means to control or implore spirits, as people who believed in such powers once did: technical means and calculations suffice, even though most of the people who benefit from them every day know nothing of how they actually work.

What has changed, then, is not each person's individual knowledge, but the collective confidence that everything, by right, is calculable by someone, somewhere, if one takes the trouble to look. The world ceased to be a cosmos populated by intentional, unpredictable forces that had to be appeased through ritual, and became a mechanism that technique and calculation can, in theory, see through entirely.

## What this shifts

Weber does not describe a dated tipping point, a precise day when the world supposedly became rational after having been magical, but a long process, under way for centuries in the West and never quite completed, a gradual evolution in what “explaining rationally” means. From explanation by wills (spirits, gods, fates) to explanation by calculable laws, the very boundary of the rational has shifted before settling, provisionally, into its current form.

This lecture, delivered to students still searching for a meaning for science after the collapse of so many prewar certainties, became one of the founding texts of the entire sociology of religion and of the theories of secularization that would follow in the 20th century. It also has its downside, which Weber accepts without hedging: a world disenchanted in his sense is also a world that has lost the capacity to answer, through meaning, the question of how to live, leaving each person facing a choice, he said, between rival and silent gods, for lack of a single oracle to rely on.

carte.punch: The world has not become more understandable: it has become calculable in principle.
carte.idee: In 1917, Max Weber names “disenchantment of the world” the shift from explanation by wills (spirits, gods) to explanation by calculation and technique. He does not say we understand the world better, only that we can, in principle, dispense with understanding it.

quiz.question: What exactly does Weber mean by the “disenchantment of the world”?
choix: That science has made the world entirely understandable to everyone
That everything is, in principle, masterable by calculation, not that everyone understands it
That religions have disappeared completely from modern society
That technology has made magic useless because it was false all along
quiz.explication: Weber insists: a city dweller generally understands electricity no better than an ancestor understood his spirits. What changes is the confidence that everything is, in principle, calculable by someone, not the actual knowledge of each individual.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what context does Weber give this lecture in 1917?
choix: Before the Berlin Academy of Sciences, for his fellow physicists
In a Munich lecture series intended for students disoriented by the war
On the occasion of his appointment as minister of education
At an international sociology congress in Vienna
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Weber addresses, on November 7, 1917, in Munich, students searching for a meaning for science after the collapse of prewar certainties, in a lecture series intended for them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the German word Entzauberung, used by Weber, literally mean?
choix: “Liberation,” in the political sense of the term
“Demagification,” that is, the removal of magic
“Acceleration,” in the sense of the pace of modern life
“Uniformization,” in the sense of cultures coming to resemble one another
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Entzauberung literally means “demagification”: the world no longer requires magical means to be mastered, which are replaced by calculation and technique.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What downside does Weber himself associate with the disenchantment of the world?
choix: The complete disappearance of every form of individual spirituality
The loss of the capacity to answer, through meaning, the question of how to live
The definitive impossibility of any further technical progress
The inevitable return to magical beliefs in future generations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Weber accepts that a world disenchanted in this sense leaves each person facing a choice between “rival and silent gods,” for lack of a single oracle to rely on in knowing how to live.
